# Principal: Juvenile used AI to make nude images of Chatham Co. charter school students & staff A minor is accused of using artificial intelligence to create nude images of students and staff at a Chatham County charter school, the school's principal wrote in a letter sent to parents.
- [artificial intelligence](https://www.wral.com/tags/artificial-intelligence/)
A juvenile is accused of using artificial intelligence to create nude images and videos of students and staff at a Chatham County charter school, the school's principal wrote in a letter sent to parents.
In the letter, a copy of which was obtained by WRAL News, Woods Charter School Principal Cotton Bryan said Chatham County deputies told school administrators that a person used artificial intelligence to transform normal photos of dozens of students and staff into nude photos and videos.
In 2024, state lawmakers [updated North Carolina's sexual extortion laws](https://www.ncleg.net/enactedlegislation/statutes/html/bysection/chapter_14/gs_14-190.13.html) to include language prohibiting the use of "artificial intelligence" as a means of producing pornographic material.

item.description:
# JudgeGPT? Artificial intelligence enters Philly judicial chambers, raising questions over accuracy. A handful of judges in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania have welcomed chatbots into their chambers. Penn researchers hope to keep the hallucinations at bay.
[Add The InquirerUs on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=inquirer.com)
Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in your search results.
![Polk Wagner at the University of Pennsylvania's Carey Law School on Nov. 2.](https://www.inquirer.com/resizer/v2/VNGXUTA6KBFSNFULZC442TG7VU.jpg?auth=795ec81a5ec9b8330cdba1e560a87b291eff5dbd2e29b6a52281fd91f96aecaa&width=760&height=507&smart=true)
Polk Wagner at the University of Pennsylvania's Carey Law School on Nov. 2. Read moreJessica Griffin / Staff Photographer
by [Jesse Bunch](https://www.inquirer.com/author/bunch_jesse/)
Published Nov. 20, 2026, 5:01 a.m. ET
Listen to article •0:00 min
A group of federal judges in Philadelphia are using artificial intelligence to aid with cases being heard in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, raising new questions about the role of AI in the region’s justice system.
The judges, participants in a pilot program run by researchers at the [University of Pennsylvania](https://www.inquirer.com/topic/university-of-pennsylvania)’s Carey Law School, have welcomed AI chatbots like ChatGPT into their chambers to schedule court hearings, draft jury instructions, and, in some cases, recall and summarize factual information about their cases. In all, around 25 judges in Pennsylvania and surrounding states are taking part.
The program, dubbed the PennLaw-Judiciary AI Testbed, provides ongoing training and support for judges and their staff as they learn about AI’s growing impact on the legal system.
Polk Wagner, a Penn legal professor who oversees the program, said participants are largely using the tools in their chambers to quicken administrative tasks, though some judges have used AI for more intensive work, such as summarizing elements of their cases and drafting documents.
“These tools are really good at compiling information on a very large scale, if you know how to use them.”
Still, changing norms around AI behind the bench raise questions about what role the technology will play in courtrooms of the future. Generative artificial intelligence is known to hallucinate, producing answers to queries that sound correct but are factually inaccurate.
In 2025, a federal judge’s chambers in New Jersey was [caught using the technology to draft an opinion that contained incorrect information and hallucinated quotes](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/two-us-judges-withdraw-rulings-after-attorneys-question-accuracy-2025-07-29/), stunning attorneys who spotted the errors. A Mississippi federal judge’s chambers made a similar blunder that year.
“People are aware of the dangers,” said Zachary Arbitman, a civil attorney and cochair of the Philadelphia Bar Association’s federal courts committee. “It’s another tool in the toolbox — you just have to use it appropriately.”
Advertisement
Arbitman said he and other attorneys continue to grapple with ethical questions over using artificial intelligence to aid their work. He was unaware that federal judges were exploring similar concerns through the Penn program.
The attorney said he is not aware of any court-wide rules on judicial AI use, noting that such technology policies typically come from judges themselves. In 2023, for example, U.S. District [Judge Michael M. Baylson issued an order](https://www.paed.uscourts.gov/sites/paed/files/documents/procedures/Standing%20Order%20Re%20Artificial%20Intelligence%206.6.pdf) requiring that attorneys who submit legal filings written with the aid of AI must disclose that they have done so.
For U.S. District Judge Joshua D. Wolson, participating in the Penn program has allowed his chambers to experiment with a tool he predicts will become intertwined with courtroom work.
Wolson, who has served in the federal civil division since 2018, said he and his staff use artificial intelligence for a variety of tasks, such as drafting charging instructions for juries before deliberations, which are often lengthy and change slightly each trial.
Advertisement
“I may have the AI help me wordsmith while I have my law clerks work on the legal analysis piece of it,” Wolson said. “Frankly, it’s faster.”
Yet Wolson said he is also mindful of the technology’s risks, refraining from using AI for tasks like legal research, summarizing documents, or drafting opinions.
Those behind the Penn program, too, say they are focused on potential concerns as they continue to enlist judicial chambers to adopt the tools.
Advertisement
To that end, Wagner, the legal professor, said his team encourages judges and their staff to keep the scope of their AI usage as limited as possible.
For more intensive uses, he said, that means ensuring that their research queries focus on specific elements of a case — dates, locations, and keywords — rather than using chatbots as a search tool for legal knowledge or judicial precedent.
“These tools are pretty bad at legal research — even today,” Wagner said, noting that the wider set of information a chatbot is asked to crawl, the increased likelihood that it could produce an inaccurate answer.
The judges taking part in the program, which has grown from fewer than 10 chambers when it began in 2024, span a range of ages and prior experience with AI, according to Wagner. While a handful of clerks have become “skeptical and hesitant” over the technology’s potential to err, he said, judges have largely reported a positive impact.
“In our view, artificial intelligence is going to be integrated into legal practice from top to bottom,” he said. “The judges realize that, and they want to make sure they and their chambers are ready.”

item.title: A statement from LPM on artificial intelligence
item.description:
# A statement from LPM on artificial intelligence It explains how we use AI and how we don't, and it outlines the standards and guiding principles behind that use.
Because AI is moving fast, people are asking questions, and the public deserves to know where we stand.
At the same time, AI is undoubtedly changing how people work and navigate their days, helping them move faster, find information quicker and solve problems that once took days, weeks and even months.
AI is the next technology of that scale.
AI is part of our new three-year strategic plan, under our priority of Digital Transformation and Adaptability.
That includes tasks like transcription, research and data analysis.
- LPM will keep innovating, experimenting and evolving to serve you better, always guided by our standards and ethics.

item.title: Building better artificial intelligence requires people willing to do meticulous work at scale
item.description:
# Building better artificial intelligence requires people willing to do meticulous work at scale "Don't make it a pilot program or a special program.
| | | |-|-| | **Guest:** | Peter Kant | | **Title:** | Founder and CEO of Enabled Intelligence | | **Summary:** | Building better artificial intelligence starts with teaching systems what they're looking at. Some workers have a unique set of skills well suited to the painstaking data-labeling work that supports AI applications across defense and the intelligence community. |
So anytime an AI software gets built or AI technology gets built, the first thing that happens to train that AI is you need people to create the data that it learns from. So people have to teach every AI, whether that’s, you know, Reddit or Facebook information or newspaper information, teaching a large language models to folks using CAPTCHA, if you’ve ever used CAPTCH and said, you know, put a box around, tell me where all the traffic lights are. And those people with AI, especially for government technology or for critical AI technology that is for critical usage, you’re important, you need high reliability and high accuracy. And so we don’t hallucinate or the AIs work functionally.
So we created as the very first stage, if someone says, hey, I’m interested in working in enabled intelligence, they go through our website and we send them an assessment and they do basically a sample labeling exercise or a data analysis exercise.

item.title: UVA President Scott Beardsley charts University’s future in artificial intelligence
item.description:
# UVA President Scott Beardsley charts University’s future in artificial intelligence President Scott Beardsley says UVA will harness the potential of artificial intelligence across the University while prioritizing responsible use and human judgment.
_On Friday, UVA President Scott Beardsley sent an email to the University community outlining his vision for the role artificial intelligence will play at UVA._
Though AI has been around for decades and has been part of the development of the internet, social media, and broadband communications, the emergence of agentic AI is accelerating the pace of transformation and sparking discussions across university campuses, including our own.
We will leverage AI technologies where they can enhance our work, productivity, and mission.
For more than three decades, UVA researchers have advanced AI and large language models. UVA offers more than 100 AI-focused courses per year and is hiring and developing faculty with a wide array of AI expertise. We are investing in the needed computing power through the new Fontaine Computing and Innovation Center and spearheading the [**Commonwealth AI Initiative**](https://ai.provost.virginia.edu/commonwealth-ai-initiative) that unites universities, industry, government, and nonprofits to establish Virginia as a source of trusted, responsible AI expertise.
This work takes place every day across disciplines and schools, including [**the first data science school in the country**](https://datascience.virginia.edu/), and at the [**LaCross Institute**](https://www.darden.virginia.edu/lacross-ai-institute) **.**
In our classrooms, labs, clinics, and offices, AI will support human judgment – not replace it.
Our graduates will use AI to sharpen their thinking – not replace it.
In the Academic Division, UVA’s [**Information Technology Services**](https://virginia.service-now.com/its?id=itsweb_kb_article&sys_id=dbe41947dbe3f91066d98f38139619db) already offers embedded AI tools such as Microsoft Copilot Chat and Google Gemini. We are committed to providing equitable access and exploring frontier AI platforms where we can learn and experiment together.
AI is shaping nearly every profession and is a trillion-dollar industry. Equally, we will promote and facilitate entrepreneurial innovation in the application of AI.
Four standing University committees on AI – for teaching and learning, research, operations, and policy and use – will advise us as this work unfolds.
**We will invest in and use AI responsibly to advance our mission.** Just as we invested in earlier generations of computing, we will pilot AI with care across our operations to drive innovation in service of our mission of education, research, patient care, and public service.
As we ambitiously advance the science and scholarship of AI, we will cultivate the human capacity to use it wisely.

item.title: House Advances Bill to Track Artificial Intelligence in Jobs
item.description:
# House Advances Bill to Track Artificial Intelligence in Jobs ## Why It Matters The [AWARE Act (H.R. 9381)](https://www.congress.gov/119/bills/hr9381/BILLS-119hr9381rh.htm), a bill directing the federal government to measure how artificial intelligence is used in the workplace, has been placed on the House Union Calendar and is eligible for floor consideration. [Tim Walberg](https://app.legis1.com/lawmaker/detail?id=51207#summary) (R-MI) introduced the measure, which would direct the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) to collect and report the data.
The bill identifies gaps in existing data on employer adoption of AI, worker-level use, changes to job tasks, training needs and effects on hiring, wages and employment.
## Partisan Perspectives Tim Walberg (R-MI), announcing the legislation on June 22, said, "W [e must have information about its impact"](https://app.legis1.com/communications/detail?id=1625397#summary) as AI transforms the workplace.
